t: Convert 20 kHz to megahertz.
e: kilo = 10³, mega = 10⁶. 20 kHz = 20×10³ Hz = 0.02×10⁶ Hz = 0.02 MHz.

t: The SI prefix 'micro' (µ) represents a multiplier of:
e: micro (µ) = 10⁻⁶. (milli = 10⁻³, nano = 10⁻⁹, pico = 10⁻¹².)

t: Which prefix means 10⁹?
e: giga (G) = 10⁹. mega = 10⁶, kilo = 10³.

t: 47 000 Ω expressed with an engineering prefix is:
Which value equals 2 200 000 Ω?
Write 0.0063 in proper scientific notation.
e: Scientific notation puts exactly one non-zero digit before the point: 6.3×10⁻³.

t: Convert 0.05 A to milliamperes.
When a prefix is made larger (e.g. kilo → mega), the numerical coefficient must:
e: Rule of thumb: bigger prefix ⇒ smaller number (and vice-versa) so the quantity is unchanged.

t: The prefix 'pico' corresponds to:
e: pico (p) = 10⁻¹² — common for small capacitors (pF).

t: Coulomb's law says the force between two point charges is:
o: inversely proportional to the square of the distance
e: F = kQ₁Q₂/r² — the force falls off with the square of the separation.

t: If the distance between two fixed charges is doubled, the Coulomb force becomes:
e: F ∝ 1/r². Doubling r multiplies the force by 1/2² = 1/4.

t: In Coulomb's law F = kQ₁Q₂/r², the constant k is approximately:
e: k ≈ 9.0×10⁹ N·m²/C². (8.85×10⁻¹² is ε₀; 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ C is the electron charge.)

t: Two charges with the SAME sign will:
e: Like charges repel; opposite charges attract.

t: Voltage between two points is best defined as:
o: the flow of charge per second
the energy (work) per unit charge between the points
e: V = W/Q — joules of work per coulomb of charge. 1 V = 1 J/C.

t: If 24 J of work moves 3 C of charge between two points, the voltage is:
Moving 2 C of charge through a 9 V potential difference requires how much energy?
e: W = QV = 2 C × 9 V = 18 J.

t: Point A is at +6 V and point B is at +2 V. The voltage across A–B is:
e: Only the difference matters: 6 V − 2 V = 4 V.

t: One coulomb is the combined charge of about how many electrons?
e: 1 C = charge of 6.242×10¹⁸ electrons (each electron is 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ C).

t: Copper conducts so well mainly because:
o: its single valence electron is loosely held and easily freed
it has a very high resistivity
e: Copper's lone valence electron is far from the nucleus → ~1.4×10²⁴ free electrons per cubic inch.

t: Electric current is defined as:
o: the rate of flow of charge (charge per unit time)
e: I = Q/t — coulombs per second. 1 A = 1 C/s.

t: If 10 C of charge pass a point in 2 s, the current is:
A steady current of 3 A flows for 4 s. How much charge passes?
How long does it take to move 6 C through a wire carrying 2 A?
e: t = Q/I = 6 C / 2 A = 3 s.

t: How are an ammeter and a voltmeter correctly connected?
o: Ammeter in parallel, voltmeter in series
Ammeter in series, voltmeter in parallel
e: Current must flow THROUGH the ammeter (series); the voltmeter reads across two points (parallel).

t: An ideal voltmeter should have:
o: the same resistance as the load
e: A voltmeter in parallel must draw ~no current, so its resistance is ideally infinite. (An ideal ammeter has zero resistance.)

t: 1 ampere is equal to:
e: 1 A = 1 C/s. (1 J/C is the volt.)

t: For a uniform wire, R = ρl/A. Increasing the LENGTH of the wire:
e: R ∝ l. A longer conductor has more resistance.

t: Doubling the cross-sectional area of a wire (length unchanged) makes its resistance:
e: R = ρl/A, so R ∝ 1/A. Doubling A halves R.

t: If a wire's length is doubled and area kept the same, its resistance:
e: R ∝ l, so doubling the length doubles the resistance.

t: In the formula R = ρl/A, the symbol ρ (rho) is the:
e: ρ is resistivity, a material property (Ω·cm in the lecture's metric units).

t: For a good conductor, as temperature rises the resistance generally:
e: More thermal vibration ⇒ more collisions ⇒ higher resistance. (Semiconductors do the opposite.)

t: A copper wire is 100 Ω at 20 °C (α₂₀ = 0.00393 /°C). Its resistance at 120 °C is about:
A 1000 Ω resistor is rated 5000 PPM/°C. Roughly how much does it change per °C?
A resistor with bands yellow–violet–orange–gold has the value:
e: Yellow = 4, violet = 7, orange = ×10³, gold = ±5 % → 47 kΩ ± 5 %.

t: Bands brown–black–red–gold correspond to:
e: Brown = 1, black = 0, red = ×10² → 10×100 = 1000 Ω = 1 kΩ, gold ±5 %.

t: On a 4-band resistor, a GOLD tolerance band means:
e: Gold = ±5 %, silver = ±10 %.

t: A three-terminal variable resistor is called a:
e: The potentiometer is the common three-terminal adjustable resistor.

t: Conductance G is:
e: G = 1/R, measured in siemens (S).

t: A 5 Ω resistor has a conductance of:
A 12 V battery is connected across a 4 Ω resistor. The current is:
e: Ohm's law: I = E/R = 12 V / 4 Ω = 3 A.

t: A 24 V source drives a 6 Ω resistor. The current is:
What voltage appears across a 10 Ω resistor carrying 2 A?
A resistor drops 20 V while carrying 5 A. Its resistance is:
On an I–V graph, an ordinary resistor produces:
o: a curve that flattens at high voltage
a straight line through the origin
e: A resistor is linear: I ∝ V, so the plot is a straight line through the origin.

t: On the I–V plot of a resistor, a STEEPER slope indicates:
e: Slope = I/V = 1/R. A steeper line means smaller R.

t: Which device has a NON-linear (curved) I–V characteristic?
e: A diode's 'resistance' depends on its operating point, so its I–V curve is nonlinear.

t: A device carries 2 A at 12 V. The power delivered is:
A 2 A current flows through a 10 Ω resistor. The power dissipated is:
How much power does a 12 V supply deliver to a 6 Ω resistor?
You know only the current I and resistance R of an element. The best power formula is:
e: With I and R known, use P = I²R.

t: One watt is equivalent to:
e: P = W/t, so 1 W = 1 J/s.

t: A 100 W lamp runs for 2 hours. Energy used (in kWh) is:
One kilowatt-hour equals how many megajoules?
Energy and power are related by:
e: Energy = power sustained over time: W = P·t.

t: Elements connected in series all share the same:
e: Series elements lie on one path, so the SAME current flows through each.

t: Three resistors 2 Ω, 3 Ω and 5 Ω in series give a total resistance of:
e: Series resistances add: R_T = 2 + 3 + 5 = 10 Ω.

t: Kirchhoff's Voltage Law states that:
o: voltage divides equally among series resistors
the sum of currents at a node is zero
the algebraic sum of voltages around any closed loop is zero
e: KVL: around any closed loop the rises and drops sum to zero (ΣV = 0).

t: In a series loop E = 12 V drives two resistors. If V₁ = 5 V, then V₂ is:
e: KVL: E = V₁ + V₂ ⇒ V₂ = 12 − 5 = 7 V.

t: Two series resistors R₁ = 2 Ω and R₂ = 4 Ω across E = 12 V. The voltage across R₂ is:
e: VDR: V₂ = R₂E/R_T = 4×12/6 = 8 V.

t: In a series circuit, the LARGEST voltage drop appears across:
e: VDR: voltage divides in proportion to resistance, so the biggest R takes the biggest share.

t: 10 Ω and 20 Ω in series across 30 V. The voltage across the 20 Ω resistor is:
A real battery has internal resistance. Under load, its terminal voltage is:
e: Load current through the internal resistance drops some voltage, so terminal V sags below the emf.

t: Elements connected in parallel all share the same:
e: Parallel elements span the same two nodes, so the SAME voltage appears across each.

t: Two resistors 6 Ω and 3 Ω in parallel give a total resistance of:
The total resistance of a parallel combination is always:
o: equal to the sum of branches
e: Adding parallel paths only makes it easier for current to flow: R_T < smallest branch resistance.

t: Two equal 100 Ω resistors in parallel have a combined resistance of:
e: Equal resistors in parallel: R_T = R/n = 100/2 = 50 Ω.

t: Kirchhoff's Current Law is based on the principle that:
o: charge cannot accumulate at a node
power is conserved in each branch
e: KCL: current in = current out at any junction, because charge can't pile up at a node.

t: Two parallel resistors, 1 kΩ and 100 Ω. Which carries the larger current?
e: Current divides inversely with resistance — the smaller resistor (100 Ω) takes the larger share.

t: 12 A enters two parallel branches R₁ = 2 Ω and R₂ = 4 Ω. The current in R₁ is:
e: Two-branch CDR uses the OTHER resistor: I₁ = R₂·I_T/(R₁+R₂) = 4×12/6 = 8 A.

t: When resistors are placed in parallel, what quantity adds directly?
e: Conductances add in parallel: G_T = G₁ + G₂ + … (so 1/R_T = Σ1/Rᵢ).

t: A Y-to-Δ (or Δ-to-Y) conversion is used when resistors are:
o: neither in series nor in parallel
e: Some bridge-like networks are neither series nor parallel; Y↔Δ conversion unlocks them.

t: Converting a voltage source E with series Rs into an equivalent current source gives I =:
e: Source conversion: I = E/Rs, with the same Rs now placed in parallel.

t: When converting between a real voltage source and a real current source, the internal resistance Rs:
e: Rs is unchanged — series with E, parallel with I.

t: An ideal voltage source has an internal resistance of:
e: An ideal voltage source holds its voltage at any current, so its internal resistance is 0 Ω.

t: In mesh (loop) analysis, assigning loop currents automatically satisfies:
e: Circulating loop currents satisfy KCL automatically; you then write KVL once per loop.

t: For a network with N nodes, nodal analysis requires solving for how many unknown node voltages?
e: One node is the 0 V reference, leaving N − 1 node voltages to find.

t: The first step in nodal analysis is to:
e: Pick a reference node assigned 0 V; all other node voltages are measured relative to it.

t: An element shared by two adjacent meshes carries a current equal to:
o: the sum of the two loop currents
the difference of the two loop currents
e: A shared branch sees BOTH loop currents, so its current is their difference.

t: Branch-current, mesh, and nodal analysis all ultimately produce:
e: Each systematic method ends in simultaneous equations to solve for the unknowns.

t: To apply superposition, an ideal VOLTAGE source that is temporarily 'turned off' is replaced by:
e: Kill a voltage source ⇒ short it (0 V). Kill a current source ⇒ open it (0 A).

t: Superposition may be used to find currents and voltages but NOT directly for:
e: Power depends on I² (or V²); squares don't superpose, so power must be found after combining.

t: A Thévenin equivalent circuit consists of:
o: a current source in parallel with a resistor
a voltage source in series with a resistor
e: Thévenin: one voltage source E_Th in series with one resistor R_Th.

t: E_Th (the Thévenin voltage) is found as:
o: the open-circuit voltage at the terminals
e: Remove the load and measure/compute the open-circuit voltage across the terminals.

t: To find R_Th, you:
o: set all sources to zero and look into the terminals
e: Zero the sources (E → short, I → open), then compute the resistance seen from the open terminals.

t: A Norton equivalent circuit is:
o: a voltage source in series with a resistor
a current source in parallel with a resistor
a resistor in series with an inductor
e: Norton: a current source I_N in parallel with R_N.

t: The Norton current I_N is the:
e: I_N is the current that flows when the output terminals are shorted.

t: How do R_N (Norton) and R_Th (Thévenin) compare for the same network?
e: R_N = R_Th — Thévenin and Norton differ only by a source conversion.

t: A DC source delivers maximum power to a load when the load resistance equals:
e: Max power transfer (DC): R_L = R_Th, giving P_max = E_Th²/(4R_Th).

t: Electric flux lines around a charged body always:
o: form closed loops with no ends
leave positive charge and enter negative charge
point from low to high potential
e: By convention E-field lines start on + charge and end on − charge, taking the most direct path and never crossing.

t: The total electric flux Ψ produced by a charge is:
o: numerically equal to the charge Q (in coulombs)
e: Ψ = Q: the flux (in coulombs) equals the charge that produces it.

t: A capacitor stores 20 µC at 10 V. Its capacitance is:
e: C = Q/V = 20 µC / 10 V = 2 µF.

t: How much charge does a 5 µF capacitor hold at 12 V?
e: Q = C·V = 5 µF × 12 V = 60 µC.

t: For a parallel-plate capacitor C = εA/d. Increasing the plate SEPARATION d:
e: C ∝ 1/d. Moving the plates apart lowers the capacitance.

t: Increasing the plate AREA of a parallel-plate capacitor:
e: C = εA/d, so C ∝ A: larger plates store more charge per volt.

t: Inserting a dielectric (instead of air) between a capacitor's plates:
e: The dielectric polarizes and partly cancels the internal field, so more charge is stored per volt → higher C.

t: The permittivity of free space ε₀ is approximately:
The relative permittivity (dielectric constant) of air is approximately:
e: εr ≈ 1 for air/vacuum; other dielectrics are higher (mica ≈ 5, some ceramics in the thousands).

t: Exceeding a capacitor's maximum (breakdown) voltage causes the dielectric to:
e: Above V_max the dielectric breaks down and conducts, often destroying the capacitor.

t: The time constant of an RC circuit is:
e: τ = RC (seconds), with R in ohms and C in farads.

t: An RC circuit has R = 10 kΩ and C = 100 µF. The time constant is:
About how long until an RC transient is considered complete?
e: After ~5τ the response is >99 % complete, so the transient is treated as finished.

t: After one time constant (1τ), a charging capacitor reaches what fraction of its final voltage?
An RC circuit has R = 2 kΩ, C = 5 µF, E = 10 V. About how long until it is fully charged?
The capacitor's defining equation is i_C = C·dv_C/dt. In steady DC this means:
e: Steady DC ⇒ dv/dt = 0 ⇒ i_C = 0: a capacitor blocks steady DC (open circuit).

t: A capacitor opposes sudden changes in:
e: Because i_C = C dv/dt, a jump in v_C would need infinite current — capacitor voltage cannot change instantly.

t: Capacitors connected in SERIES all share the same:
e: The same charging current for the same time puts the SAME charge on each: Q_T = Q₁ = Q₂ = Q₃.

t: Two capacitors 6 µF and 3 µF in series give a total capacitance of:
e: Series caps combine like parallel resistors: C_T = (6×3)/(6+3) = 2 µF.

t: Two capacitors 6 µF and 3 µF in PARALLEL give a total of:
e: Parallel capacitances add: C_T = 6 + 3 = 9 µF.

t: Compared with resistors, capacitors combine:
o: in the opposite way (parallel adds, series by reciprocals)
e: Capacitors are the mirror image of resistors: parallel adds, series uses reciprocals.

t: The energy stored in a capacitor is:
e: W_C = ½CV², stored in the electric field between the plates.

t: Energy stored in a 100 µF capacitor charged to 50 V is:
Magnetic flux lines:
o: always point toward the south pole only
e: Magnetic flux lines are continuous closed loops (N to S outside the magnet, S to N inside).

t: Flux density B is given by:
e: B = Φ/A (teslas); 1 T = 1 Wb/m².

t: The permeability of free space µ₀ is:
e: µ₀ = 4π×10⁻⁷ Wb/(A·m).

t: Ferromagnetic materials (iron, nickel, steel) have a relative permeability µr that is:
e: Ferromagnetics have µr ≫ 1, hugely concentrating flux — but they saturate at high flux.

t: Magnetic 'core saturation' means that beyond some point:
o: the core resistance drops to zero
extra current produces almost no extra flux
e: Once saturated, the core's domains are aligned, so more current barely increases the flux.

t: In L = N²µA/l, the inductance depends on the number of turns as:
e: Inductance grows with the SQUARE of the number of turns (note the N²).

t: Faraday's law states the induced voltage in a coil is:
e: e = N dΦ/dt — the induced voltage is proportional to turns and the RATE of flux change.

t: According to Faraday's law, a steady (unchanging) magnetic flux through a coil induces:
e: No change in flux (dΦ/dt = 0) ⇒ no induced voltage.

t: Lenz's law states that an induced voltage/current always acts to:
o: aid the change that produced it
oppose the change that produced it
e: Lenz's law: the induced effect opposes the change in flux that caused it ('nature dislikes change').

t: The inductor's defining equation v_L = L·di_L/dt means that in steady DC:
e: Steady DC ⇒ di/dt = 0 ⇒ v_L = 0: an inductor looks like a short circuit to steady DC.

t: An inductor opposes sudden changes in:
e: Because v_L = L di/dt, inductor current cannot change instantly.

t: An RL circuit has L = 2 H and R = 100 Ω. The time constant is:
At the instant a switch closes on an RL circuit, the inductor initially behaves like a(n):
e: Current cannot jump, so i_L starts at 0 (open) and the full supply voltage appears across L.

t: When the switch OPENS on an inductive circuit, the collapsing field can produce:
o: a voltage spike much larger than the supply
e: Inductor current insists on continuing; forced through a high resistance it generates a large reverse voltage spike (sparks).

t: Inductors in series (no coupling) combine:
o: as the product over the sum only
e: Inductors combine exactly like resistors: series adds (L_T = L₁ + L₂ + …).

t: Two inductors 6 H and 3 H in parallel (no coupling) give:
e: Like parallel resistors: L_T = (6×3)/(6+3) = 2 H.

t: In steady-state DC (after transients settle), replace each element as follows:
e: Steady state: inductor → short (v_L = 0), capacitor → open (i_C = 0).

t: Energy stored in a 0.5 H inductor carrying 4 A is:
Which statement correctly pairs the energy formulas?
e: Capacitor stores ½CV² (via voltage); inductor stores ½LI² (via current).

t: The 'period' (T) of a sinusoidal waveform is:
o: the time for one complete cycle
the number of cycles per second
e: T is the time of one full cycle, measured between any two corresponding points.

t: The peak-to-peak value of a pure sine wave equals:
e: From negative peak to positive peak = 2 × amplitude for a symmetric sine.

t: A lowercase symbol such as v or i denotes the waveform's:
o: instantaneous value at a particular moment
e: Lowercase = instantaneous value; capital subscripted (V_m) = peak.

t: Frequency and period are related by:
e: f = 1/T (hertz); 1 Hz = 1 cycle per second.

t: A waveform has a period of 20 ms. Its frequency is:
e: f = 1/T = 1/0.020 s = 50 Hz (European mains).

t: The period of a 60 Hz waveform is about:
How many radians are there in 360°?
e: A full circle is 2π radians = 360°.

t: 90° expressed in radians is:
One radian is approximately:
Angular velocity ω is related to frequency by:
e: ω = 2πf = 2π/T (rad/s).

t: The angular velocity of a 50 Hz waveform is approximately:
e: ω = 2πf = 2π×50 ≈ 314 rad/s. (377 rad/s corresponds to 60 Hz.)

t: At 60 Hz, the angular velocity ω is about:
e: ω = 2π×60 ≈ 377 rad/s (the classic 60 Hz value).

t: In v = V_m sin(ωt + θ), a POSITIVE angle θ means the wave:
e: +θ shifts the sine left so it reaches its peak earlier → it leads.

t: Given v = 10 sin(ωt + 30°) and i = 5 sin(ωt − 30°), the voltage:
o: is in phase with the current
e: Phase difference = 30° − (−30°) = 60°, with v ahead → v leads i by 60°.

t: Two waveforms compared for phase must have the same:
e: Lead/lag is only meaningful between waveforms of the same frequency.

t: The useful identity relating cosine and sine is:
e: cos x = sin(x + 90°): a cosine leads the corresponding sine by 90°.

t: The average value of a complete sine cycle is:
e: Equal positive and negative areas cancel, so a full sine cycle averages to zero.

t: For a sine wave, the RMS (effective) value equals:
A sinusoidal voltage has a peak of 311 V. A voltmeter (RMS) reads about:
e: V_rms = 0.707 × 311 ≈ 220 V — European mains.

t: If a sine current has an RMS value of 10 A, its peak value is about:
European mains is quoted as 230 V (RMS). Its peak voltage is about:
Unless stated otherwise, an AC voltage or current value is assumed to be the:
e: By convention, unlabeled AC quantities are RMS — that's what meters read.

t: The RMS value is defined by matching the AC waveform's:
o: peak voltage to a DC source
heating (power) effect to an equivalent DC value
e: RMS = the DC value that produces the same average heating/power.

t: In a purely RESISTIVE AC circuit, voltage and current are:
e: A resistor's v and i rise and fall together — in phase (opposition R is frequency-independent).

t: In a purely CAPACITIVE AC circuit:
e: i_C = C dv/dt → current leads voltage by 90° (ICE).

t: The memory aid 'ELI the ICE man' tells you that:
o: in L, current leads voltage; in C, voltage leads current
in L, voltage (E) leads current (I); in C, current (I) leads voltage (E)
e: ELI: in an inductor E leads I. ICE: in a capacitor I leads E.

t: Inductive reactance is given by:
e: X_L = ωL = 2πfL (ohms).

t: X_L of a 0.1 H inductor at 60 Hz is about:
As frequency increases, inductive reactance X_L:
e: X_L = 2πfL grows in direct proportion to frequency (a straight line from the origin).

t: Capacitive reactance is given by:
e: X_C = 1/(ωC) = 1/(2πfC) (ohms).

t: As frequency increases, capacitive reactance X_C:
e: X_C = 1/(2πfC) is a hyperbola: higher f → smaller X_C (the cap approaches a short).

t: X_C of a 10 µF capacitor at 60 Hz is about:
At DC (f = 0), an ideal inductor behaves like a ___ and an ideal capacitor like a ___:
e: X_L = 0 at DC (short); X_C → ∞ at DC (open).

t: At very HIGH frequency, an ideal capacitor approaches a:
e: X_C = 1/(2πfC) → 0 as f → ∞, so the cap approaches a short circuit.

t: A complex number written as X + jY is in:
e: X + jY is rectangular form; Z∠θ is polar form.

t: The magnitude of the complex number 3 + j4 is:
Convert 3 + j4 to polar form:
Complex numbers are easiest to ADD or SUBTRACT in:
e: Add/subtract in rectangular form (combine real parts, combine j-parts).

t: Complex numbers are easiest to MULTIPLY or DIVIDE in:
e: In polar form: multiply magnitudes & add angles; divide magnitudes & subtract angles.

t: A phasor represents a sinusoid by a:
e: A phasor is a frozen rotating vector — a complex number capturing magnitude and phase.

t: When a time-domain sinusoid is converted to a phasor, the phasor magnitude is usually taken as the:
e: Phasors normally use RMS magnitudes: V = 0.707 V_m ∠θ.

t: Impedance Z is best described as the AC generalization of:
e: Z is a complex 'resistance' — its magnitude opposes current and its angle sets the v–i phase shift.

t: The impedance of an ideal inductor is written as:
e: Z_L = jX_L = X_L∠90°: voltage leads current by 90°.

t: The impedance of an ideal capacitor is:
e: Z_C = −jX_C = X_C∠−90°: current leads voltage by 90°.

t: Impedances connected in series:
e: Z_T = Z₁ + Z₂ + … , just like resistors but with complex arithmetic.

t: For a series R-L-C circuit, the total impedance is:
e: Z_T = R + j(X_L − X_C): the reactances oppose each other on the j-axis.

t: A series circuit has R = 6 Ω, X_L = 10 Ω, X_C = 12 Ω. The total impedance is:
e: Z_T = R + j(X_L − X_C) = 6 + j(10−12) = 6 − j2 Ω. Negative j-part ⇒ capacitive.

t: A series circuit has R = 3 Ω, X_L = 8 Ω, X_C = 4 Ω. The magnitude of Z_T is:
If the source CURRENT leads the applied voltage, the network is predominantly:
e: Current leading voltage is the capacitive signature (ICE). Voltage leading ⇒ inductive.

t: Which DC techniques carry over to AC by simply replacing R with Z?
o: KVL, KCL, VDR, CDR, mesh, nodal, Thévenin, Norton — all of them
e: The lecture's central message: every DC method works in AC using complex impedances and phasors.

t: Real (average) power in an AC circuit is:
e: P = V_rms I_rms cos θ — only the in-phase component does real work.

t: The average power consumed by an IDEAL inductor or capacitor over a full cycle is:
e: A pure reactance returns all energy it stores each cycle, so its average (real) power is zero.

t: A load draws 5 A (RMS) at 120 V (RMS) with a power factor of 0.8. The real power is:
e: P = V_rms I_rms cos θ = 120 × 5 × 0.8 = 480 W.

t: Apparent power S is given by S = V·I and is measured in:
e: S = V_rms I_rms, in volt-amperes (VA) — what the source must supply.

t: The power triangle relates S, P and Q by:
e: S² = P² + Q²: apparent power is the hypotenuse of the right triangle.

t: A load has P = 80 W and Q = 60 VAR. The apparent power S is:
Reactive power Q is measured in:
e: Q is in VAR — power swapped back and forth with L/C fields, never consumed.

t: Power factor is defined as:
e: F_p = cos θ = P/S — the fraction of apparent power doing real work.

t: The power factor of a purely resistive load is:
e: Resistive ⇒ θ = 0 ⇒ cos θ = 1. A pure L or C has F_p = 0.

t: A 'lagging' power factor indicates a predominantly ___ load:
e: Lagging = current lags voltage = inductive. Leading = capacitive.

t: If P = 80 W and S = 100 VA, the power factor is:
To correct the lagging power factor of a motor, you typically add a:
e: A parallel capacitor supplies the reactive power locally (Q_C cancels Q_L), raising F_p toward 1.

t: The instantaneous power p = vi in a resistive AC circuit pulses at:
e: p = vi for a resistor is always ≥ 0 and oscillates at twice the line frequency.

t: At series resonance, the total impedance is:
e: With X_L − X_C = 0, Z_T = R — its minimum value — so the circuit looks purely resistive.

t: At series resonance, the current drawn from the source is:
e: Minimum impedance (= R) ⇒ maximum current I = E/R.

t: At resonance the circuit's power factor is:
e: Purely resistive at resonance ⇒ v and i in phase ⇒ F_p = 1.

t: The series resonant frequency is given by:
e: Setting X_L = X_C gives ω_s = 1/√(LC), so f_s = 1/(2π√(LC)).

t: If both L and C are doubled, the resonant frequency f_s:
e: f_s = 1/(2π√(LC)). Doubling both makes LC ×4, √(LC) ×2, so f_s halves.

t: At series resonance, V_L and V_C individually are:
o: equal and opposite (they cancel in the loop)
e: V_L and V_C are equal in magnitude but 180° apart, so they cancel — leaving E = V_R.

t: A series resonant circuit has X_L = 480 Ω and R = 6 Ω. Its Q_s is:
A high quality factor Q means the resonant circuit is:
e: High Q ⇒ narrow bandwidth ⇒ very selective (good for picking one station).

t: A series resonant circuit with Q_s = 80 is fed 10 V. The capacitor voltage at resonance is about:
e: V_C = Q_s·E = 80 × 10 = 800 V — the famous resonant voltage rise.

t: At series resonance, the voltage across L (or C) compared with the source voltage is:
o: Q times larger (can far exceed the supply)
e: V_L = V_C = Q·E. With high Q these element voltages can be many times the supply voltage.

t: The bandwidth of a resonant circuit is the band between the frequencies where the current falls to:
e: The half-power points are at 0.707 I_max (since P ∝ I², 0.707² = ½).

t: Bandwidth relates to resonant frequency and Q by:
e: BW = f_s/Q_s = R/(2πL). High Q ⇒ narrow band.

t: A circuit resonant at 10 kHz has Q_s = 50. Its bandwidth is:
The half-power frequencies of a resonant circuit are 90 kHz and 110 kHz. The resonant frequency f_s (geometric mean) is about:
Half-power points are so named because at those frequencies the power delivered is:
e: At 0.707 I_max, P = I²R falls to (0.707)² = 0.5 of the peak power.

t: At parallel (tank circuit) resonance, the impedance seen by the source is:
e: Parallel resonance is the dual of series: impedance is MAXIMUM (current from source is minimum).

t: At parallel resonance, the current drawn from the source is:
e: Maximum impedance ⇒ minimum source current. Energy circulates inside the L–C loop.

t: Compared with a series resonant circuit, a parallel resonant circuit has:
o: the opposite impedance behaviour (max where series is min)
e: Parallel resonance flips every series behaviour: Z max ↔ min, I min ↔ max.

t: In an ideal parallel resonant 'tank' circuit, at resonance there is a large:
o: circulating current between L and C
e: Energy sloshes back and forth between L and C; the source only replaces the losses.

t: A transformer transfers energy from primary to secondary by means of:
e: AC in the primary makes changing flux; by Faraday's law that induces voltage in the secondary — no electrical contact.

t: Mutual inductance between two coils is given by:
e: M = k√(L_p L_s), where k is the coupling coefficient (0…1).

t: The coefficient of coupling k for a tightly-coupled iron-core transformer is close to:
e: Iron cores give k ≈ 1 (nearly all primary flux links the secondary); air cores are much lower.

t: Two coils with L_p = L_s = 2 H have a coupling coefficient k = 0.5. The mutual inductance M is:
Two coupled coils in series combine as L_T = L₁ + L₂ ± 2M. The +2M (aiding) case occurs when:
e: Use +2M when the mutual fluxes aid, −2M when they oppose.

t: L₁ = 4 H, L₂ = 4 H, M = 1 H, connected series-aiding. The total inductance is:
For an ideal transformer, the voltage ratio equals:
e: Voltages scale WITH turns: E_p/E_s = N_p/N_s = a.

t: In a transformer, the current ratio is:
e: Currents scale INVERSELY with turns (energy is conserved): I_p/I_s = N_s/N_p.

t: A transformer has N_p = 200, N_s = 50 turns. Its turns ratio a is:
e: a = N_p/N_s = 200/50 = 4 (a step-down transformer for voltage).

t: A 4:1 step-down transformer has 120 V on the primary. The secondary voltage is:
A turns ratio a < 1 (more secondary turns than primary) gives a transformer that:
e: a = N_p/N_s < 1 means N_s > N_p, so the secondary voltage is higher → step-up.

t: A load Z_L on the secondary appears at the primary terminals as:
e: Reflected (primary) impedance Z_p = a²·Z_L.

t: An 8:1 transformer (a = 8) drives an 8 Ω speaker. The amplifier 'sees':
A transformer with a = 10 has a 4 Ω load on its secondary. The primary sees:
Which is NOT one of a transformer's three main uses?
e: Transformers change voltage, isolate, and match impedance — but they do nothing with steady DC (no changing flux).

t: “The algebraic sum of the currents entering and leaving a junction of the network is zero.” This is:
e: This is the statement of Kirchhoff's Current Law (KCL).

t: “The current through, or voltage across, any element of a network equals the algebraic sum of the currents or voltages produced independently by each source.” This is the:
e: This is the definition of the superposition theorem.

t: The definition of 1 volt is properly described by which equation?
e: 1 volt = 1 joule of energy per 1 coulomb of charge: V = W/Q = J/C.

t: Coulomb's law for the force between charges Q₁ and Q₂ separated by a distance r is:
e: Coulomb's law: F = kQ₁Q₂/r² — the force varies inversely with the square of the distance.

t: How many electrons must pass through a copper wire in 1 second to produce a current of 1 ampere?
e: 1 A = 1 C/s and 1 C = 6.242 × 10¹⁸ electron charges, so 6.242 × 10¹⁸ electrons per second.

t: What is the starting mechanism of current flow in a circuit?
o: the magnetic field of the Earth
e: An applied voltage (potential difference) is what sets the free electrons into orderly motion.

t: A higher value of a resistor's temperature sensitivity [ppm/°C] means:
o: the resistance changes more for a given change in temperature
the resistance is independent of temperature
the resistor has a lower power rating
e: ppm/°C is the temperature coefficient: a higher value ⇒ a larger change in resistance per degree of temperature change.

t: Convert 0.0047 mF to picofarads (pF).
For an IDEAL capacitor, what is the value of the energy DISSIPATED when a voltage is applied to it?
e: An ideal capacitor STORES energy (½CV²) in its field but DISSIPATES none, so the dissipated energy is 0.

t: For the charging phase of an R-C network, the capacitor current i_C is given by:
e: During charging the current starts at E/R and decays: i_C = (E/R)·e^(−t/τ).

t: The relative permeability (µ_r) of diamagnetic materials is:
e: Diamagnetic materials have µ_r slightly less than 1 (they weakly oppose the field).

t: If you move a conductor through a magnetic field at right angles to the flux, you generate a(n):
e: Motion of a conductor through magnetic flux induces a voltage (Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction).

t: The reactive power Q can best be described as:
o: the power dissipated as heat in resistors
power alternately absorbed and returned by the reactive (L/C) elements, not consumed
the total power supplied by the source
the product of RMS voltage and current
e: Reactive power is exchanged with the magnetic/electric fields of L and C each cycle — stored and returned, never net-consumed (units VAR).

t: The maximum value of a waveform measured from its average (mean) value is called the:
e: Measured from the average level to the maximum is the peak amplitude (V_m).

t: Which expression does NOT describe the (average) real power of a sinusoidal waveform?
e: Average power uses cos θ. V_rms·I_rms·sin θ is the REACTIVE power Q, not the real power.

t: A transformer with turns ratio a = 2 drives a 4 Ω load. The impedance seen at the primary (reflected impedance) is:
An ideal transformer with turns ratio a = N_p/N_s is correctly described by:
e: Voltages scale WITH turns (E_p/E_s = N_p/N_s); currents scale INVERSELY (I_p/I_s = N_s/N_p).

t: In the network theorems, an independent current source is replaced by ___ when it is deactivated:
e: A deactivated (zero) current source passes no current -> it becomes an open circuit. (A voltage source becomes a short.)

t: According to the definition, the electric field strength is described by which formula?
e: Electric field strength E = F/Q - force per unit charge (N/C).

t: According to the definition, a capacitance is described by which formula?
e: Capacitance C = Q/V - charge stored per volt (farads).

t: The energy stored by an inductor can be described as:
e: An inductor stores W = ½LI² in its magnetic field.

t: The time constant of an R-L circuit is described as:
e: For an R-L circuit, τ = L/R seconds.

t: When an initially uncharged capacitor begins to charge, its equivalent behaviour at the very first instant is that of a:
e: With no charge yet, v_C = 0, so the capacitor momentarily acts as a short circuit (current = E/R).

t: The resonant condition of an RLC circuit is described as:
e: At resonance the reactances are equal: X_L = X_C, so they cancel and the circuit is purely resistive.

t: The quality factor Q of a series resonant circuit is given by the general formula:
e: Q_s = X_L/R = (reactive power)/(average power) at resonance.

t: The phase relationship between voltage and current for an inductor is:
o: voltage and current are in phase
voltage leads current by 90° (current lags by 90°)
e: For an inductor, v_L leads i_L by 90° (ELI).

t: According to the maximum power transfer theorem (AC), maximum power is delivered to the load when the load impedance is:
o: the complex conjugate of the Thévenin impedance
e: For AC, Z_L = Z_Th* (the complex conjugate) - same resistance, opposite reactance - so the reactances cancel.
